To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the heating rate induced by light absorbing aerosols (HR) is a function of the season, the daily cycle, the cloudiness, and the source, and (2) the heating rate of brown carbon (HRBrC) is 12.5% of that of black carbon (HRBC) and is 87.5% of the total heating rate induced by the light absorbing aerosols.
the HR of LAA is 1.04 K day-1 (summer) to 1.83 K day-1 and 0.43 K day-1 to 1.75 K day-1 under clear and overcast conditions, respectively.

the heating rates of light absorbing aerosols (HR) are (1) highest in the morning, (2) higher in the winter than in the summer, (3) higher in clear than in cloudy skies, (4) higher in biomass burning (BB) than in fossil fuel (FF) emissions, (5) dominated by black carbon (BC), and (6) dominated by the direct aerosol absorption rather than by the diffuse and reflected light absorption.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) the development of a novel methodology for the measurement of the HR induced by LAA, (2) the quantification of the seasonal, diurnal, and cloudiness variability of HR and its apportionment to sources and LAA components, and (3) the experimental determination of the HR of BC and BrC in the Po Valley.
the quantification of the HR induced by LAA and its apportionment to sources, species and cloudiness.
the quantification of the HR induced by LAA, which can be used to assess the impact of LAA on the climate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the heating rate is higher in winter and in clear sky conditions, and that the heating rate of black carbon is much higher than that of brown carbon.
LAA heat the atmosphere, and this heating is higher in the winter, in the morning, and when the sky is clear.
the HR of LAA in the Po Valley is 1.83 K day-1 on average, and it is dominated by BC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LAA heating rate is higher in winter, in the morning, and in clear sky conditions; that the heating rate is dominated by BC; and that the heating rate of BrC is comparable to that of BC.
HRBC is the main contributor to LAA heating, followed by HRBrC, and HRBB, while the contribution of dust is negligible.
the heating rate of the light absorbing aerosols in the Po Valley is 1.04±0.01 K d-1 in summer and 1.83±0.02 K d-1 during the winter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HR of LAA is strongly affected by clouds and that the apportionment of HR to different aerosol species and sources is strongly dependent on the sky conditions.
HR is a highly variable quantity and its quantification requires time-resolved measurements.
the HR of BrCs can be measured and that its contribution to total aerosol heating is non-negligible.
